title: DNS Extensions to Support IP Version 6
summary: Defines the changes the Domain Name System needs so that hosts running IPv6 can be found by name. It introduces a new record type for IPv6 addresses and a way to look up a name from an IPv6 address. It was replaced by RFC 3596.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC extended DNS to store IPv6 addresses and look up names from those addresses. It introduced the AAAA record and the IP6.INT reverse-lookup domain, but it has since been obsoleted.

questions: what is the aaaa record type number
how did dns add ipv6 support
subtitle: The original DNS extensions for storing and looking up IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: DNS applications assumed address queries returned 32-bit IPv4 addresses, making IPv6 address support difficult.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1886 defines the AAAA record for a 128-bit IPv6 address, the IP6.INT reverse-lookup domain, and additional-section processing for A and AAAA records.
tldr.outcome: This Historic RFC is obsoleted by RFC 3596 and updated by RFCs 2874 and 3152.

today: RFC 1886 is Historic and obsoleted by RFC 3596. The unit metadata also lists updates by RFC 2874 and RFC 3152.

sections.title: DNS Changes for IPv6
sections.content:
Applications expected DNS address queries to return 32-bit IPv4 addresses, so IPv6 support needed new definitions. RFC 1886 keeps existing IPv4 support and adds extensions for IPv6.

The extensions define a record mapping a domain name to an IPv6 address, a domain for address-based lookup, and changes to some queries' additional-section processing.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS originally expected short IPv4 addresses. This RFC added rules so DNS could also store and return IPv6 addresses while retaining IPv4 support.

sections.title: The AAAA Resource Record
sections.content:
The AAAA record is specific to the Internet class and stores one IPv6 address. Its type value is 28 decimal, and its address data is 128 bits in network byte order.

A host with more than one IPv6 address needs more than one AAAA record. An AAAA query returns the associated records in the answer section and does not perform additional-section processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Each AAAA record stores one IPv6 address for a name. If a host has several addresses, it has several records.

sections.title: Reverse Lookup with IP6.INT
sections.content:
The RFC defines IP6.INT as a domain for looking up a name from an IPv6 address. It represents the address as hexadecimal nibbles in reverse order, separated by dots and followed by .IP6.INT.

The example address 4321:0:1:2:3:4:567:89ab is represented by reversing its nibbles in the corresponding IP6.INT name.
sections.plainLanguage: For a reverse lookup, the address's hexadecimal digits are written one at a time in reverse order under IP6.INT. DNS can then look up the name associated with that address.

sections.title: Additional Address Records
sections.content:
NS, MX, and MB queries that already perform additional processing for type A records are redefined to process AAAA records as well.

A name server adds locally available IPv4 and IPv6 addresses to the additional section of responses to these query types. The memo says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: Some DNS responses can include both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses for the names they mention. The memo does not discuss security issues.
